newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU harmonises inflation data before EMU decision.
newsitem.headline: EU harmonises inflation data before EMU decision.

text.p: The European Commission, preparing for the single currency, releases for the first time on Friday comparable inflation data designed to help to determine which countries qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

European Union leaders will use the harmonised consumer price indices when they decide in early 1998 which countries fulfil the condition on price stability, one of five economic criteria which must be met for joining EMU.
Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, and the national statistics agencies have worked together to harmonise the way inflation is measured to make the figures comparable.
Friday's statistics will cover January and Eurostat will then publish such data every month. The decision on which countries qualify for EMU will be based mainly on data for 1997.

"They are important in the sense that these are the numbers that will form the basis for the judgment on whether countries meet the inflation criterion," said David Walton, co-director of European economic research at investment bank Goldman Sachs.
Later in the year, it will become increasingly clear which countries will meet the price stability requirement. "They will gain in importance as the year progresses," Walton said.

According to the Maastricht treaty, a country's average inflation rate over a year should not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of, at most, the three best-performing member states in terms of price stability.
The harmonised figures may well differ from those published nationally as methods of compilation differ. This could prove to be important when deciding which countries meet the requirement.
For example, the British harmonised figure, released already last month, was 2.2 percent year-on-year in January, much lower than the increase in the official retail price index of 2.8 percent.
"They may well be quite a bit different," said Walton.
Economist Ellen van der Gulik at JP Morgan said the Dutch rate of inflation could be 0.4-0.5 percentage points lower than the nationally published January rate of 2.3 percent.

She would also be looking closely at the Spanish and Italian figures. "To me Spain is very important because I think that Spain is very likely to meet all the criteria, the only tricky one is inflation," van der Gulik said.
However, also the harmonised figures are expected to show that most EU countries are on track to meet the price criterion.

"The general picture for the market will not change dramatically by this because the developments of inflation in Europe have in the recent past been one of the success stories in European convergence," said Theodor Schonebeck, economist at Deutsche Bank research.
Excessive price rises are not expected to be an obstacle to creating EMU. "Inflation is really at the moment not the problem we have in Europe and this is confirmed every month," he said.
Last November, the European Commission estimated that 14 countries had a good chance of meeting the inflation requirement in 1997 -- all member states except Greece.
This contrasts with the great difficulties countries such as Germany and France have in cutting their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, another EMU condition.

There is still some uncertainty, however, concerning the application of the inflation criterion. For example, in a report last November the European Commission used six different ways of calculating the inflation rate which must not be exceeded.
"Here, the Maastricht treaty leaves a lot of room for interpretation," said JP Morgan's van der Gulik.
But regardless of the method used, the same countries were at the time found to meet the price stability criterion.

Van der Gulik also said there was disagreement among the national statistical offices on how to measure consumer prices in, for example, the fields of health and education. These categories would not therefore be included in the harmonised indices.
"In all, therefore, it is still difficult to be confident about which countries will satisfy the price criterion early next year," she said.
